The changes to the Act will allow it to perform much better. When the situation changed regarding the volumes of grain that we were shipping, we were very pleased. When the inflation rate increased much more rapidly than we had anticipated in 1975 and 1976, it became obvious to us that the Bill which was passed by the House at that time was not performing according to the basis upon which it was passed. It was meant to stabilize the cash flow of the Prairie economy. When the cash flow decreased stabilization payments were to be made in order to allow the Prairie economy to perform more adequately. That happened. It began in 1981 with rapid inflation and high costs of production as a result and world prices of commodities stabilizing and decreasing. It continued through 1982 and 1983 and into this year.
Yet, because of the complex formula which was put in place to trigger this Bill, stabilization payments were not being made. Farmers were asking their Members of Parliament why they were not receiving payments when they had contributed to this fund with the good faith that it would assist them when financial difficulties were being experienced in the Prairies. We told them why. We also told them that it could only be changed through legislation. It was the law of the land that the formula which was in place in the Bill in 1976 was still in place. It had to be followed until it was changed by the House of Commons. Until today we could not persuade the Government to bring forward this Bill. That is why we had meetings on the Prairies. That is why we exerted pressure in the House to have the Bill brought forward.
I looked back at the speeches that were made in 1976, and I even found one that I had made at that time. I enjoyed reading them. I also noted the points that were made by the Member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) and the Member for Red Deer. They have both already spoken on this Bill. At that time they were looking into the future as they do so well. They were seeing that these difficulties were possible. They were concerned about them. They said that maybe we should amend this Bill to make it closer to a kind of insurance stabilization Act so that the whole Prairies would not be affected. If there was a drought in southern Saskatchewan and the rest of the Prairies had a bumper crop, they wanted the Act to be applied. That seemed like a reasonable suggestion. They asked that the Committee travel to learn the experiences of farmers. That was accepted. They also asked that the legislation be placed under the control of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). That has never been accepted. It seems that the growing of wheat and the sale of that wheat is being placed in the hands of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy). That is why we had the interesting Crow legislation brought into the House by the Minister of Transport.
What happens now that the grain farmers recognize the complexities of this Bill? They are recognizing that the cost of transportation of grain will be a great addition to their cost of production this year. The one thing which Prairie farmers
Western Grain Stabilization Act
knew was a constant in the production of grain was the cost of transportation. It remained the same. They could count on that. Today that constant has been removed. As of this August the cost of moving grain on the Prairies will be 58 per cent higher than last August. Yet when the Minister of Transport pushed this Bill through the House he said that we have a safety net. He said that we would protect the Prairie farmers from large increases in freight costs. It is 10 per cent of the cost of transportation. In small print it was suggested that that was the average of six grains, and it was based on the volume of the shipment of those grains. It is now evident that as freight rates increase 58 per cent for the price of moving the grains that do not bring as much money as canola, for example, they can pay 58 per cent more than last year and the safety net does not even come into effect. That is a lot of protection for the farmers of western Canada.
As I said at the beginning of my speech, the pressure is on Members of all Parties in the House to pass this Bill. The reason is that as farmers scramble to find cash to stay alive in the difficult economic times, the only pool of money available to them is that money which they have contributed to the Western Grain Stabilization Fund. When they look to another source, the indicators are not very good.
We talked about farm fuels as one of those negative indicators, as noted by the Hon. Member for Red Deer. There is an increase of some 50 cents to 68 cents per gallon in the cost of farm fuels that is taken by the federal Government. We have called for the removal of that for well over two years to assist farmers and to put a positive indicator before them instead of a negative one. That would assist in the production of grains which brings so much capital to this country.
Today in Question Period I pointed out that the Farm Credit Corporation is again increasing the interest rates for loans to farmers. That increase is at least one per cent to 1.5 per cent above what farmers can obtain from chartered banks. The Farm Credit Corporation is supposed to be the lending institution to which farmers can go as a last resort to obtain loans to continue farming or expand their operations. Again, this is another negative indicator from the Government.
Members of the House have introduced Private Members' Bills in an attempt to alleviate the situation, by promoting the removal of the sales tax on farm fuels and the use of agribonds to help in lowering interest rates for farmers. These attempts were stalled in committee by the Government because it is not prepared to deal with these issues. It is finally starting to move ahead slowly, but the Finance committee is smothered with budget bills.
In western Canada Wheat Board sells the farmers' grain and is responsible, with the assistance of the Minister responsible for the Wheat Board, for establishing the initial price which farmers will receive when they deliver their grain to the elevator. There is no encouragement from the federal Government here.

May 25, 1984
Western Grain Stabilization Act
The Minister does not say that the Government will support the farmer this time by not lowering the initial price below what it was last year because the cost of production has gone up. He will not say that the federal treasury will stand behind the Wheat Board if necessary because grain prices do not increase in the international market. Again, there is nothing from the federal Government. In fact, there was a lowering of initial prices to the farmers. Many farmers are beginning to wonder how they can continue to produce as they continue to get negative indicators from the international community and their own national government.
In addition to all of this, there is an increase in the freight rate which they must pay to get their commodity to the market. This increase which they must pay to the railways, because there are very few options, will increase by 35 per cent to August 1, and 58 per cent after that all in this one year. The Government will allow the addition of $25 million to that freight bill as the cost of shipping higher volumes of grain than forecast from August 1, 1983, to December 1, 1983. This cost will not be borne by the Government-the Bill was not even passed until the end of the year-but will be added to the freight rate costs.
Furthermore, the railroads have made a submission to the Canadian Transportation Commission asking for revisions to the cost of capital formula. They were offered $100 million as the cost of capital for moving grain. Now that the Bill is passed and they have the $651 million in their possession, they are going before the Transport Commission asking to boost that cost of capital to $250 million. I hope the CTC does not allow that because, if it does, that will add an additional cost to the transporting of grain of $3 a metric tonne.
I recently read an interview with Mr. Lawless of the CNR which appeared in the Western Producer. I could hardly believe what I read. He was lamenting the fact that there were no incentives to the railroad to improve service to the farmers. He said that this money just meets their cost of production and that there is no incentive to change the system at the ports to put a looping in the tracks so that cars could continuously unload, or to install unit trains which would assist farmers in the Prairies. He said that there was no incentive to do that. The complaint was that the railways must load the grain from all of these prairie elevators and that there is no money there to somehow assist supporting the tracks to those Prairie elevators.
As I read that interview, it seemed that the President of the CNR was saying that after the Crow Bill was passed, giving the railroads the costs for moving grain, there was still no incentive to increase their efficiency in moving the farmers' grain. I want to say to him that if $300 million is not sufficient to provide the efficiencies that are needed on the Prairies and to keep the costs to the farmers down, then I do not know what is.
I am only sorry that the Minister who is bringing this Bill to the House today, who was the Minister of Transport at that time, was not allowed to remain in that portfolio. I am convinced that western farmers would have received a better
deal if he had been allowed to stay. I am convinced that he understood what the commissioner who was appointed at that time was saying about what was needed on the Prairies to move grain. I am convinced that he would have fought, with our support, for at least a partial payment to the producers to keep the railroads efficient. I am convinced that the Agricultural Stabilization Fund of $204 million, which he put in that Bill, would have been in place now to assist farmers with the extra transportation costs.
He was being very kind today when he said that they put the good animals out to greener pastures. I had hoped that the Government would keep him on and let him pilot this Bill through, because I think we would have had a better deal. However, we have a Minister from Western Canada, and what do we have? There is a great deal for the railroads; and we can see why because we know who he is supporting.
I want to conclude by saying that we are prepared to do everything possible to pass this Bill. We want to allow the Government to make the interim payment which we indicated was essential. The amendments to this Bill will receive our quick scrutiny in committee. We hope that this Bill will pass and allow western farmers some money to put their crops in the ground; that nature will assist those farmers and world prices will not be depressed so that they can look to a bright future. They are the basis upon which the western economy grows.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: There follows a ten minute period for questions or comments. Continuing debate. The Hon. Member for the Battlefords-Meadow Lake.

Mr. Speaker, I have a few comments for the record on second reading of Bill C-33, an Act to amend the Western Grain Stabilization Act. It is with some interest that I noticed the introduction of the debate today by the Minister for External Relations (Mr. Pepin) who was Minister of Transport when the abolition of the statutory Crow rate took place. I must say that in the Minsiter's speech today he portrayed a great deal of understanding about the plight of the western Canadian grain farmers and the desperate situation in which some of them find themselves today. I only wish he had shown that kind of understanding and empathy for the western Canadian grain farmer when he pushed the abolition of the statutory Crow rate through the House of Commons, one of the last few subsidies our grain farmers had.
Beyond that, it is even more surprising to me that many speeches delivered by Conservative Members have criticized the Liberal Government for allowing the Crow rate to be dismantled. I remind them that if we had had the adequate support we called for from all Opposition Members of the House I do not think the Liberals would have been able to put through Bill C-155 which changed the statutory Crow rate and which has put farmers in an ever worsening economic situation in western Canada.
May 25, 1984

The Western Grain Stabilization plan was introduced in 1976. At that time the New Democratic Party, from their speeches I have looked at, warned that there were several factors which would not allow the plan to meet farmers' expectations, mainly because the formula was based on market price rather than cost of production. It included the entire Prairie area. It also used the calendar year rather than the crop year, and it ignored the greater grain volumes on gross incomes. The plan failed to make a pay-out when needed. That is basically the bottom line.
Many farmers in my area were quite enthusiastic about the Western Grain Stabilization Plan when it was first introduced. As the Minister of the day said, it would be designed so that if there were a bad crop year, payments would be made in the spring to assist farmers with spring operations, seeding and the associated higher costs at that time of the year. For almost five years there have been no pay-outs made under the Act, even when large numbers of farmers have been in dire straits.
Economic conditions are not looking that good for Western farmers. This is the same for people right across Canada, but I am more familiar with the situation of grain farmers in areas like The Battlefords-Meadow Lake. Part of the reason is that the cost of grain production has gone up dramatically. Just take a look at fuel costs, interest rates, machinery prices, fertilizer costs and chemical costs, Mr. Speaker. Then there is the cost of harvesting. All of these costs have gone up astronomically over the past number of years, while at the same time the average price of all grains over the past few years has gone down continually. On many occasions farmers are caught in a situation whre they do not get back even their cost of production because of the economics of grain farming. That does not take into account the possibility of not having rain at the proper time, a too early frost, or too wet a spring. These are the difficult situations faced by grain farmers.
Because many places have been producing more, many parts of the Prairies have felt that the Western Grain Stabilization fund should have triggered a pay-out. Their net income has not increased; in fact it is dropping. But because of increased production,-more sales I suppose is a more accurate way of putting it-a payment under this program has not been triggered and that is unfortunate, Mr. Speaker. Farmers are being penalized under this program for their efficiency in growing greater volumes of grain. They see their work is not being rewarded because they do not get the economic return they deserve.
In the four or five years during which there has been no payment from the fund, the fund has continued to increase. Every farmer that is registered, and that is about 75 per cent of the grain producers in western Canada, pays a percentage of all grain sales into the fund. That payment used to be, I believe, 2 per cent. For the last year it has been 1.5 per cent. For every dollar generated by this checkoff the Government has a responsibility under the present Western Grain Stabilization Act of putting $2 of public revenue into the fund. Farmers have contributed a little over $300 million. This means the Government has put in over $600 million, and there
Western Grain Stabilization Act
is now a net amount in the fund of between $900 million and $1 billion. That is a lot of money, Mr. Speaker. Farmers have a hard time understanding, now that they are in bad economic straits, why they cannot get money out of the program.
We are very happy in the New Democratic Party to see this Bill in the House to change the Western Grain Stabilization Act. We think the Bill has some pitfalls. We feel there should be some further action taken now that the Bill is before the House. Our intention is to see the Bill move rapidly into committee where we can make amendments in addition to those which the Government has already indicated it is willing to accept to change the Bill. I believe there is one further amendment which the Minister spoke of when he introduced the Bill this morning.
Farmers do not just need the money now; they needed that money a couple of months ago. Opposition members pushed the Government very hard to bring in the Bill. I do not know whether the Bill was not drafted, or whether there was not enough room on the Order Paper, but farmers needed that money before, not sometime in the future.

speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
speechtext: Everything is either too early or too late. It is never right.

Nevertheless we are happy to see the Bill in the House now. We want to see an immediate payment go out to the western Canadian grain farmers. There are some amendments we feel should be made to this Bill. I hope they will receive the support of the Official Opposition as well as the support of the Government. First, we would like to see payments retroactive to 1983. Second, we would like to see an interim pay-out for the 1983 crop year. I think the Minister said in his introduction this morning that the Government had in mind an amendment for the 1983-84 year. I hope that comes to pass. Third, we would like to see some recognition of the regional discrepancies within the Western Grain Stabilization plan. We have been calling for recognition of crop discrepancies as well as regional discrepancies. Finally, there should be some recognition of the net incomes of farmers in the pay-out under the Western Grain Stabilization Program. We feel, as we felt back in 1976 when the plan was introduced, that there should be a tie-in with the cost of production. There should be recognition of the fact that the cost of production is a major factor in any stabilization program. Also we are recommending that there be immediate pay-out guarantees.
Hopefully we will get the Bill through the House today and into committee, and hopefully there will be some debate in good faith on the amendments to which we would like to obtain the agreement of the Government and the Official Opposition. If we cannot accomplish that, so be it. I think we have put forth the true feelings of grain farmers in western Canada. If the other Parties will not go for it, at least we in the NDP know that we have made adequate representations on behalf of western grain farmers.

May 25, 1984
Western Grain Stabilization Act
In the Bill the time period over which averages are taken has been reduced from five years to three years. This is something for which Hon. Members, such as the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) and the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo), have pushed many times during debates in the House of Commons. They have pushed for changes to the Western Grain Stabilization Act.
Some three months ago the New Democratic Party released a policy paper on agriculture which contained what we consider to be alternate proposals for grain income stabilization. We agree with the Canada Grains Council that a plan amalgamated with crop insurance should be tailored to individual needs, sensitive to individual income fluctuations and to regional discrepancies. That is the best way to proceed. We still feel that is the best way after much discussion within our own caucus and with farming people across the country. Unfortunately the Government does not agree. I hope it will give consideration to some of the amendments we will put forth in committee and that we have speedy passage of this Bill.
In terms of an income insurance plan, we would like it to be actuarially sound, voluntary and attractive. It should be attractive so that all farmers, whether big or small, involved in co-operative or partnership farming, or whatever, become involved and see it as a benefit. If we opened up the Western Grain Stabilization Program and allowed people to leave it, I am sure there would be a mass exodus, unless some of the changes we have recommended in the House of Commons today and in previous debates are implemented. Although I recognize that the changes of the Government are an improvement, they are certainly not tailored to the needs of western Canadian grain farmers. There would be an exodus of people from that plan unless it is tailored to meet their needs.
Another feature of the program could be participation by producers, the federal and provincial Governments. The income insurance plan would be as integrated as possible with the existing crop insurance program to avoid duplication in the recordkeeping and administrative services necessary to carry out an adequate program of this magnitude, especially in terms of its impact upon the western economy and upon the Canadian economy in general.
The federal contribution would be in the form of reduced premiums that people would have to pay for the program. The provincial contribution would be primarily to expand the crop insurance administrative capability to meet the requirements of an income insurance plan. It would generate a greater volume of work for those who administer the plan at the present time. I would like to see the federal Government talking with the provincial governments about crop insurance programs to see if they would be willing to take on a greater responsibility to meet the needs of farmers within their respective provinces.
Finally, we recommend that farmers be able to insure for both volumes shipped and market price. A variety of insured price levels would be offered with appropriate premium levels to reflect the wide variation in production costs.
Those are a few examples of what we in the New Democratic Party think should be in place as an alternative to the Western Grain Stabilization Program. In fact, we would be very happy if Hon. Members of the Government and of the Official Opposition would at least debate and consider in committee the value of our suggestions, and our policy on agriculture as it pertains to the Western Grain Stabilization Act. If these suggestions were accepted, we would have a program much better tailored to the needs of western Canadian grain farmers than what we have had in the past.
In closing, I appreciate the opportunity to participate in this debate today. I hope government Members will take note of our suggestions, given as constructive criticism to improve the program and meet the needs of a sector of the economy about which we are very concerned. Hopefully Bill C-33 will move out of the House and into committee at the end of the debate today. Then we can look at some of the changes and, hopefully, give it speedy passage, so that farmers who need money to continue their operations will receive it as soon as is viably possible.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Are there any questions or comments relating to the Hon. Member's remarks? Debate.

Mr. Speaker, I must say at the outset that the Bill before us is both important and serious. However, the chance of giving a false impression with respect to it is dangerous. It is easy to conscience people who are following this debate on television, or will be reading it in Hansard or perhaps Members of the House of Commons, that we are debating a Bill which is aimed primarily or solely at western Canada. Although the primary emphasis of the Western Grain Stabilization Program is to feed money back to Canadian farm producers on the Prairies, this Bill will have an impact upon all Canadians-food consumers as well as industrialists who purchase western Canadian products. It must be seen in the light of its importance as a national Bill.
Bill C-33 gives too little too late; it is too pompous and too political. It is too little because it is less than the investment of farmers in the stabilization plan. It is too late because it comes considerably after the period of sowing crops, when cash flow was needed prior to seeding. It is too pompous because the Government stood on its pedestal and released a nine-page press release to the nation. It is too political because it comes on the eve of an election.
With nearly $1 billion in the Western Grain Stabilization Fund, farmers do not even get back their own money. They have contributed almost one-third of the investment in the fund today, but what will be given back to them will be in the neighbourhood of only $300 million.
Today different people have referred to the Minister as the Minister for External Relations or as the Minister for external affairs. I hope the Minister knows the difference between affairs and relations.
May 25, 1984

speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
speechtext: It is more of the same.

I say to the Minister in all seriousness that it would have been better had the farmer taken his money and invested it elsewhere, even in bank savings. Had the farmers taken that amount of money they could have accumulated since 1979 somewhere in the neighbourhood of $8,000, had they invested it other than in the Western Grain Stabilization Fund. On the basis of that investment, they are being shortchanged by this Government. This Government would try to convince farmers that if they pulled their teeth without anaesthetic it would be good for them. This Bill is like building a three-wire fence to keep birds out. It does not offer the farmers the protection they believed they were buying in 1976.
It is important to talk about the philosophy of the Western Grain Stabilization Plan and the reason such stabilization is necessary today. Canadians know that farm producers have existed in this country since the very first person arrived on the North American continent. What is significantly different in the last half of this country's existence are the changes in the economic dynamics of agriculture, such that farmers today can no longer afford to have a crop loss.
As a Member of Parliament who was born and raised on a farm, and had some experience with the great depression years, I find it interesting that at that time, as in all previous times in history of the world up until the recent past, depressed times do not drive people off farms. In fact, the depression drove people to the farms. The pictures of people riding the boxcars in the thirties do not show people flooding to the cities. Those were city dwellers riding the boxcars back to the farm. On the farm their brother, uncle or some other relative had a cow, a chicken and a pig. Bessie gave milk, the chicken gave eggs, and the pig provided pork. They had a vegetable garden. Once the farmland was paid for, you could not starve them off it.
The nature of agriculture has significantly changed. We are into specialized industries, single commodity production. Input costs have risen so dramatically that agriculture today simply cannot afford a crop failure. We are still in the same cycle of boom and bust. We should not interfere with that cycle. It is the natural market forces at work. The farmers expected that the Western Grain Stabilization Plan would be a system of equalization so that in boom years they could put money aside and in the bust years they could draw upon that account and have some stability in their industry.
What do we have in 1983 and 1984? We have the absolute epitome of bust. What do we get from this Government? We get a year of delay in bringing about a system of payment. The Government has the cock-eyed notion that somehow the formula could not be changed sooner, even though it knew it had the support of the Opposition Parties. It would have been a simple one-day procedure to make that change. Instead, they bring it out on election eve for political gain. What a sinister fact to put before western grain farmers. As I said before, this is not just a farm issue. There is not a single person in this
Western Grain Stabilization Act country who does not eat daily. Farming today is not a lifestyle. These are business people in the business of food production.
We need to readdress the whole concept of agriculture. Looking at the world facts, there is no industry as important as farming. Four-fifths of the world population suffers from malnutrition, 70 million per year suffer permanent and irreversible brain damage from lack of protein and 40,000 children a day die of starvation. That was 40,000 children yesterday, 40,000 today and 40,000 tomorrow.
Against that background, there is not one nation in the world that gives top priority to agriculture. In this country, as in many other countries, ranking along the lowest priorities are agriculture, Fisheries and forestry. This world will one day wake up to the fact that it is not the industrial centres that make this country tick.
I know why we are in this kind of situation. Most farmers in Canada know why this is the case. In Canada there are more Members of Parliament from Montreal and Toronto than there are from Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, Northwest Territories, Yukon and British Columbia, excepting the Fraser Valley and City of Vancouver, combined. The people in two cities have more voting power as to how this country is run than those in 70 per cent of our land mass. They are nice people in Montreal and Toronto. You, Mr. Speaker, might be from that area.
Your leader comes from there.

My Leader does come from there, but he is advantaged. One-third of his caucus comes from the Prairies and represent western farming. There are 21 Members of Parliament from Alberta. The Liberal Party of Canada has 21 Members in eight provinces and two territories. The balance are from Quebec and Ontario.
The Member says that my Leader comes from Montreal. However, he has the influence of Prairie people who feed people in Montreal and Toronto. He has respect for the Western Grain Stabilization Plan. That is why he stood in this House of Commons to raise the issue with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). It became a national issue. It was only then that we got action on the Western Grain Stabilization Plan. The Hon. Member says that is right. My Leader has a sensitivity for the issue. Now it is being resolved, unfortunately a year and a half too late.
Farmers all across this country, not just in the west, are receiving commodity prices equal to those of 1973, but their input costs have increased since that time by 150 per cent. Agriculture Canada tells us that by 1988, just four years from now, they will go up another 110 per cent. What a devastating set of conditions. My friends to my far left, the NDP, would not allow any labour group to fall so far behind. However, the food producers who feed this whole country-and we should bear in mind there are only two sources of food, soil and water-have fallen behind with input costs increasing 150 per cent, and another 110 per cent projected by 1988, with virtually every commodity price falling. That is the devastating

May 25, 1984
Western Grain Stabilization Act background upon which this Government rests its case for agriculture.
There should be no interim payment. An interim payment is indicated for July. There should not be one. Full payment should have been made many months ago. Rather than an interim payment in July the whole payment should be made. All one need do is look at the accounts of the Farm Credit Corporation which show that farm bankruptcies are up well over 100 per cent from those of just a year ago when farm bankruptcies had greatly increased over the year preceding that. Those figures do not at all take into account those farmers who, out of pride, managed to get out of the farming business before they had to register for bankruptcy. They, Sir, comprise the larger number of persons. I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the agricultural industry must be seen for what it is.
Canadair has received S3 billion and de Havilland has received $270 million. If that kind of money were given to the agricultural industry it would yield returns to the nation of somewhere in the neighbourhood of $9 billion to $10 billion. The multiplier factor in relation to agricultural dollars is 3.5, because we know for sure that farmers do not keep their money, they spend it. As soon as a farmer is finished buying his machinery, he buys a refrigerator. That is the reason this is an issue which affects all of Canada.
When a farmer buys a combine, a tractor or any farm implement, it is in all likelihood made in central Canada. If a farmer decides to buy a new car, and it is a Canadian car, it is in all likelihood made in central Canada. If he buys a new refrigerator for his wife's kitchen, it is in all likelihood made in central Canada. The agricultural dollar has the greatest multiplier effect of any dollar in any industry in the entire country. That dollar use will multiply 3.5 times. If some of the money that was spent for the protection of de Havilland and Canadair had been given to the farmers, I submit that this country would be better off.
Lest I be misinterpreted, I am not saying that those industries to which I have referred are not industries that ought to be supported. That is not the case I am laying before you, Mr. Speaker. The case I am laying before you, Mr. Speaker, is that we cannot justify such enormous support for industrial sectors while blindly eating food every day in the belief that we will forever more have cheap food on our tables, unless we as a nation give greater support to the agricultural industry. That support may take the form of higher prices or, alternatively, of lower input costs.
Farmers today require the ability to manage without having decade-old cash receipts along with input costs that are increasing by 150 per cent. I beg this nation to recognize that there is no country in the world, not even the United States of America, that enjoys less costly food than Canada. We spend less of our disposable income on food than any other nation in the world. The last time I studied that question, and I concede at the outset that that was a year or two ago, I found that Canadians were then spending 18 per cent of their disposable
income on food. I do know that Canadians spend less of their average take-home pay on food than Americans. That simply will not continue to be the case, and urban people will have to face the fact that they will have to pay more unless they recognize the agriculture is an industry and the farmer is a businessman who is in the business of food production.
The farmers paid into the Western Grain Stabilization Plan in order to even off boom and bust years. After procrastinating, and being prodded by the Opposition Parties for a year and a half, the Government has finally come through in its dying hour, just before Parliament is about to prorogue for an election, giving the farmers less than they invested, without giving back any of what the Government had contracted to give them. I tell you, Sir, that record is despicable. It is despicable to treat agriculture in such a devastating way.
The truth of the matter is that urban people as well as farmers need to know that the bill before us is one that affects all Canadians. Based upon that, Sir, I as a western Canadian find it both humorous and sad that every single candidate in the Liberal leadership race has shown up in western Canada saying that they will put a new face on western issues. They have all said: "We are out here to tell you that we will take into consideration your aspirations, your wants and your needs." We have heard that before, Mr. Speaker. We heard that during the 1968 leadership convention.
Whenever there is a Liberal leadership race, the candidates run all over every acre of our land telling us that we are wonderful people and that they need us. They do not need to tell us that, Sir. We know that they need us because they eat food every day and they need food products. However, we hate to be treated in the manner in which we are being treated. The farmers are paying into a fund which has accumulated nearly $1 billion while the Government procrastinates through years and years of bust. Then finally in the dying hours of the Government, right before the election, farmers are told that they will receive a portion of their money back. If anyone thinks for one moment that a farmer will walk over to a Liberal leadership candidate, kiss his ring and say: "Thank you, Sir, you have saved my farm," he is wrong, because that farmer has a tool out in his barnyard with three times that will express very well exactly what he thinks of such Liberal leadership candidates. Those candidates will become a part of the legacy of the great Otto Lang. I notice that there is a picture of Otto Lang's skull at the entrance to the Parliamentary Restaurant. There is a picture of all of the Liberals in western Canada there as well. There are pictures of them in the museum which is in the riding of the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor). They are called the dinosaur species and they are dinosaurs; not because they have cruel hearts but because the country has paid attention to the affairs of urban Canada without concern for the regions and without the realization that food is an industry the same as manufacturing is an industry. Those dinosaurs believed that food would always be there and that food would always be cheap.
The Western Grain Stabilization Plan must be made more sensitive on a continuing basis. It must make its pay-out now
May 25, 1984

because the need for it is now. There is no reason for the delay. I see that you are signalling that my time is up, Mr. Speaker. The issue is certainly not dead.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Are there any questions or comments?
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Hon. Member who sits right beside me, although he is a member of the other Party.
Thank goodness.

speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
speechtext: So close yet so far.

I would like to say on the record that it is not true that I have had discussions about joining the Conservative Party. I know that the Hon. Member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn) has been leaking this news all over the country, but it is not true.
The Hon. Member who last spoke is a thoughtful and philosophical Member in spite of the fact that he is a member of the Conservative Party. It used to be that 40 per cent, 50 per cent or even 60 per cent of the people in the workforce were farmers. Now, after the great industrial revolution and continued technological change, I believe that 3 per cent, 2 per cent or even 1 per cent of the people are employed on the farms.

speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
speechtext: Five per cent.

It is 5 per cent. A small percentage of the workers are working on the farm. The Hon. Member was complaining as I sometimes do about the influence of these bad easterners over here with all of their power who put it to the poor western farmers. I would like to ask the Hon. Member how he sees the western farmers having more power or even adequate power to take care of their own interests when they seem to comprise a declining percentage of the workforce in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I only got as far as page 2 of my notes, and I had about 12 pages I wanted to present. It is very simple. What we need is an elected Senate with equal representation from every province in the country. I am not saying that the Senate should have absolute legal power over the House of Commons. I recognize the principle of one person one vote. But the truth of the matter is that it is equally wrong today to have a situation in which Toronto and Montreal can out-vote 70 per cent of Canada's land mass.
If we had a magical chain-saw and could cut Toronto out and throw it away, the hinterland resources are such that within a decade we would build a new Toronto. If we cut the hinterland out-with its forestry, mineral rock, agricultural lands and fresh water-and threw it away, Toronto would be dead within a year. We need to bring into balance and perspective the management that takes place in our nation between the fewer people in the resource-based areas and those
Western Grain Stabilization Act who utilize the resources of the urban centres. An urban person does nothing except help manage resources. That is what the banks, the insurance companies and all the rest of the institutions are there for. It all relates back in some way or other to the resource base. If that was not there, the urban centres would not be there.
The prejudice and bias against farmers is there because of provincial governments. They will charge urban people $5, $6, or $7 for a private telephone line, while farmers who have to buy $100,000 combines have to share their telephone lines with four of their neighbours. This is evident in the postal system. Urban people can go out in their pyjamas on Sunday morning, reach around the corner and get their newspaper and letters. They can do that any day of the week. Farmers have the privilege of renting a postal box for $10 a year. This pertains to in communications and other areas.
I would simply say to my hon. friend from Vancouver-Kingsway that this country needs an elected Senate so that we can start to do as the American people do; to talk about "us" and "we" instead of being Canadians talking about "I" and "them". I would submit that there is more difference between a person from Texas and a person from Boston than there is between one from Toronto and one from Edmonton. Yet, the divisions of our country exist there because we have never brought the regions into balance. In answer to my hon. friend's question, we must bring some regional balance into the political system.

Mr. Speaker, I must take this occasion to rise on a question of privilege as I have been accused of being from Toronto by the Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone). I must point out that there are farmers in my constituency.
Second, I must ask whether the Hon. Member was speaking with tongue in cheek when he said there were no cities in western Canada and no people in cities in western Canada, or that the people who are in cities are nothings. Doe he mean that the people who live in Vancouver, Calgary, Edmonton, Winnipeg, and Saskatoon are nothings? Surely he has speaking with tongue in cheek when he said that.
Finally, did the Hon. Member seriously put forth the propo-sotion that those Ministers who have represented western Canada-Minister Olson, Minister Argue and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) who is recognized for his reputation as being sensitive to farming interests-are not sensitive to western needs?

Mr. Speaker, if I had suggested that the Hon. Member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Crosgrove) was a Torontonian, I truly apologize to him. I did not mean in any way to do that to him.
On the other hand, with respect to the suggestion that I said that people in cities were nothings, I do not know if I said that. I cannot remember saying that. I will read Hansard. If I did say that, that was certainly not my intention. Every human being everywhere is important, is an important resource of the country. All people are somebodies. That is what we want to have in this country; people who are somebodies.

May 25, 1984
Western Grain Stabilization Act
With respect to the Ministers the Hon. Member claims are great Ministers, who are protecting western Canada-and he singled out as one example the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan)-he asked if I might have been submitting that thought tongue in cheek. If I was trying to suggest that the Minister of Agriculture was indeed protecting western Canada, my tongue would have been right through my cheek and half a dozen other cheeks. He is the person who wants market supply management for our beef industry. Even good old NDP Manitoba voted 80 per cent against that concept. I could tell the House about all the protection that has been provided to western Canada, but my time is used up and I cannot go on with this speech any longer. I will tell you flat out, Mr. Speaker, they would not stand a chance, with the philosophies they have about agriculture, of getting elected anywhere in any constituency west of the Manitoba-Ontario border by a group of farmers. Not a single one of them.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: On debate, the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker).

Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief in order to give Members opposite a chance to speak on this Bill. I would like to say a few words, however, as I was a member of the agriculture committee in the mid-seventies and travelled throughout western Canada.
I think that this Bill, which has been agreed to by all Parties, is indeed a good Bill. The amendments to the Bill are attempting to enforce what the original Bill intended. I think that is a fair statement. I will not go through all of the positive features of the Bill, although perhaps I should. Members opposite have not addressed their remarks entirely to the Bill, but have stayed somewhat to the intent of the Government in introducing the Bill. I agree with Members opposite that it should not take such a long time to bring in a Bill such as this. The previous speaker said that it should only take a day. Certainly, it should not take two months as one opposition Member suggested. If it took four months, it would be outrageous. If it took six months it would be more than outrageous. It should certainly not take eight months. But I am wondering what happened when the Conservative Party was in power for eight months. Why was something not done then if it could have been done in one day? That is point number one; to even out this argument about timing. No matter what is brought in by the Government-even if it is good legislation-the Opposition say there is something politically bad about it, and speeches are delivered in the House which take away from the general thrust and intent of the legislation.
There were three or four Members opposite who referred to other costs that primary producers have. Primary producers are the most important people in this country today. They are the people who keep the country alive and on a sound footing-the fishermen, farmers, people who work in the forests and people who work in the mines. But, whenever the subject is brought up it becomes entirely political.
For example, when Members discussed the costs to Canadians, one Member said that the people of Canada were led
astray with the 18-cent increase in the price of gasoline that the Opposition wanted to bring in and, of course, the dollar that they claimed the Liberals brought in. As a matter of record, the only difference between both major Parties in this country is that the Liberal Party was preaching 75 percent world prices and the Progressive Conservative Party was preaching 100 per cent. That is the only difference. For someone to say that such and such a person pays an extra 50 cents or 60 cents, directly or indirectly, in fuel taxes is not the question. The question is the total amount of money they pay for oil and gas in this country. I agree that the present taxes on oil and gas for primary producers should be eliminated. That is both provincial and federal taxes, and they vary from province to province.
At the same time let us recognize that it would be very strange to hear a Member from western Canada say that we should have lower oil and gas prices right across Canada. Go speak to the Premier of Alberta and ask him whether he agrees with that. For that matter, go to the Premier of my province, the poorest province in Canada, and ask him if he agrees with that. Every time the price of oil and gas rises $1, equalization payments from the federal Government shoot up $100 million. Therefore, when you talk about prices being paid by Canadians for oil and gas, it should be looked at in its totality and the Canadian people should not be mislead.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: What Bill are we talking about, Mr. Speaker? There should be relevancy on both sides, not just this side.

The other argument is that the timing is wrong. They say that the Liberal Government is bringing it in just prior to a federal election. There is not a farmer in western Canada, Mr. Speaker, who would say no, do not bring it in because there is an election coming up. He does not care if there is an election or not. What he wants is this Bill brought into the House. I could go on about that but I will not.
Another point of condemnation of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) and members opposite seemed to be somewhat irate, was that the Minister is bringing in an amendment at committee stage to give the farmers a payment now. As I said, I do not know as much as I should know about farmers in this country, but on checking I understand that the Minister is not only bringing in this amendment, he is also attempting to have these payments made the first week in June, not the last of July as was mentioned in the Chamber. The Minister is bringing in this amendment, which Members opposite as well as farmers wanted and asked for, and he should be praised by Members opposite for doing so. Whether or not there is an election is totally immaterial. It will be absolutely ludicrous to follow that line of reasoning because, if you did, you would not bring in any good legislation at all prior to an anticipated election.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Wait until I make my fish speech, then you will be really impressed.
May 25, 1984

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Are there any questions or comments?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Are you kidding? It is not worthy of questions.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Debate. The Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor).

Mr. Speaker, the only comment I have about the remarks of the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) is that they are just a year and a half late. It took a year and a half for them to get it into their heads that the farmer needed money. Look how many farmers went bankrupt in 1983. They could have been on the land today had the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the Government listened to the Hon. Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson) and our leader. They begged and entreated the Government to do something to save the farms of the West. But the Government took a year and a half to do it. Sometimes I think we should do a little more research on birds so that we could cross a homing pigeon with a woodpecker. We could use them here to send a message over to them and it could be pounded into their heads. They would not have to take a year and a half to do something while 400 farmers are going bankrupt.
This Government has stacked the cards against western Canada for years.

speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
speechtext: Come on.

Yes, you have. I will give you a couple of instances. The farmers know it. You are not going to fool anyone out there. At least I do not think you are going to fool very many, if any, by giving them a payment of their own money just before the election.

speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
speechtext: We are not trying to do that at all.

That is exactly what you have in mind. If there was not an election coming we would have to wait another year and another 400 farmers could go bankrupt. That is how much the Government cares about western Canada. We get the dirty end of the stick all the time. For years we have had the dirty end of the stick.
In this Bill the Minister says we are now going to let them opt out. I thought we had freedom of choice in this country. That is what the Charter says. Now the Government is going to give us permission to opt out every ten years. What is more, there is no provision to pay the money back when the farmer opts out. The Government is going to keep his money. Talk about Moscow! This Government is worse than Moscow. At least over there you know you are not going to get it back, but here you expect the Government to be democratic and pay it back when you opt out. What nonsense. How naive do you think farmers in western Canada are? They have paid $5,000 to $8,000 into this fund and they are just going to drop out and leave it in the pockets of the federal Government to spend in extravagant ways? Our farmers are not naive. They are well
Western Grain Stabilization Act educated people and when they want to opt out they want their money back, every red cent of it, and the interest it earned. If this Government has any morality at all-

speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
speechtext: Louder.
-any morality at all-

speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
speechtext: Louder!
The Minister says they have not. I believe that, but if there is any morality at all they will make an amendment and pay back the farmer the money the Government has taken from him.
Hear, hear!

If you pay something and you do not get the goods, the money is refunded. But here the Government has a new idea. It will keep the money. Let them opt out but they will not get their money back. It is getting worse and worse, Mr. Speaker. Talk about stacking the cards against the people of the West! The Government did it in the capital cost allowance. Look at what the budgets have done to western Canada.
Not only has the capital cost allowance provision put thousands of people out of work, it has forced farmers to keep their old antiquated equipment. One dealer alone had to cancel seven combines because the Government said it will not let the farmer have his capital cost allowance in the first year because be buys the machine in August. Who in the world is going to buy a combine in January when you do not use it until August or November? That is how the Government looks on western Canada. I wish some of the unemployed and some of the farm machinery companies in the East would wake up and know what is going on. This Government is responsible for a great number of them being unemployed through its policies, and the capital cost allowance is only one.
Talk about western Canada getting the dirty end of the stick. Look at the capital gains tax. The only pension a farmer has is his farm. Then the Government brings in the capital gains tax and taxes the farmer on half of the gain. He will no longer be able to go and buy a home in the city. If they could do that additional housing would be required. People would have to build houses and that would create employment.
We wonder why there are two million unemployed in the country. It is because of Government policy. How many people has the Government put out of work in these two instances alone? The capital gains tax is the only pension that farmers have. We make them stay on the farm when they would like to sell the farm. We even tax them on the inflated value of the farm. Of course the Government made a change for bond holders. The bond holder does not have to pay capital gains tax on the inflated value of his bonds. However, the poor farmer who lives in western Canada has to pay on the inflated value of his farm. That is money he has never had. This is another case,

May 25, 1984
Western Grain Stabilization Act Mr. Speaker, in which we are getting the dirty end of the stick. There are many such cases we could deal with today.
At the end of his speech today the Minister gave us a wonderful message. He said he is going to do what Progressive Conservative Members and the Leader of our Party have been asking him to do from the beginning. He is going to pay out the money so that it can be used for spring seeding. The money was needed for spring seeding. Some farmers have not seeded yet because they have run out of credit at the banks. They have no more land to put up for another loan. They are either getting their friends to seed it or are not seeding at all. In May he says he is going to make an interim payment before the end of July. Do Hon. Members on that side of the House realize that crops have to be seeded in May if they are going to be harvested before the frost in the fall? You cannot wait until the first of August to plant your crops because you will then have the money to do it. That is absolute nonsense.
They are not even going to bring this change in at committee. They are going to blackball the committee and bring it in at report stage so that it cannot be debated. There will be no people there to say what they think about it. That is a wonderful, smart idea. I wonder who stayed up all night to dream that up. Mr. Speaker? There is no reason why that change should not be made in committee where it can be debated so that we can get the payment as fast as possible, rather than after a tremendous delay.
The calendar year is going to help, Mr. Speaker, but it is not going to make a great deal of difference in the triggering of pay-outs. It is going to make some difference and we thank you for that little crumb.
Why were the other things we suggested not brought in, such as the cost of machinery and production? Why is every cost of production not considered rather than only the ones set out in the Act? Some of the biggest costs of production, such as inflation and interests, are not included. They say they are going to change the Act by using the calendar year. That is another crumb. This money belongs to the farmers, Mr. Speaker. They are not getting back even the amount they paid in. Do not try to kid the troops. We know what is going on. One-third of the total amount of $900 billion belongs to the farmers.

speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
speechtext: Indeed, one-third. You said it.

Their interest is in that too. The total payment in 1978 was only $369 million. In those days the Government did have some honour. It said that $123 million came out of the farmers' pockets and they gave it back. The Government said it contributed $246 million and it would not give that amount back. The total was $369 million and they told the farmers that they were going to get $123 million plus the Government's share, including the interest they earned. Once it is put into that fund it is no longer government money. It belongs to the Western Grain Stabilization Fund which belongs to the farmers of western Canada. Do not try to kid the troops and tell us we are getting back more than we put into the fund. If you say that in western Canada you will be
driven out of the hall and tarred and feathered. The farmers will just not go for that kind of nonsense. Now the Government says the farmers may get $350 million out of the $900 million-almost $1 billion. That is not even one-third of the total amount, and we may not even get that.
It is no wonder that only one of a mast number of farmers who came to a meeting in Strathmore a few weeks ago would not opt out. The rest of the farmers wanted to opt out immediately, but they want their money back. They are not going to make a gift of their money to the Government. They should be getting their money back.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I will say that if the Government does not have the morality to pay money back to a farmer when he opts out, then we have left democracy behind us and are at the bottom of the garbage pail. It is no wonder that the whole group of farmers at Strathmore wanted out. Now the Government is going to be very nice. It will let them out in 1986 but will not return their money. I hope that some of the reasonable minds on that side of the House will awaken and pay back the money when a farmer opts out, or change the Act so that it will do what it is supposed to do, stabilize the incomes of western Canada.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions or comments? The Hon. Member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnaty-shyn) on debate.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am looking at the clock and I see that only a very short period of time remains. I have had informal discussions with the Government House Leader. We had hoped to hear from a few speakers today, and we intend to have this Bill pass second reading today. I was wondering whether there could be a disposition to not see four o'clock, which would give me a few minutes to make a few concluding comments on behalf of my Party with respect to this particular legislation. If that were acceptable to everyone in the House, I would like to say a few words since this affects my district very seriously.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would agree to that provided that the House will adjourn at five o'clock in any case. speechtext: The House resumed, from Tuesday, January 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. Anguish, that Bill C-203, an Act to declare Canada a Nuclear Weapons Free Zone, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence.

Mr. Speaker, I am particularly happy to rise today to speak in favour of Bill C-203, an Act to declare Canada a Nuclear Weapons Free Zone, not only because I fully support both the principle and the letter of the Bill before us, but also because my constituency of Kootenay-West has had on a number of occasions over the past year and a half the highest percentage totals on disarmament referenda within Canada, one of those votes for disarmament being as high as 99.7 per cent in one of our component electoral districts. Also, some half dozen cities and villages within Kootenay West's boundaries have declared themselves as nuclear free zones either by resolution or by

by-law. I am also particularly pleased to speak on this Bill because it is authored by my colleague, the Hon. Member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake (Mr. Anguish) from the Province of Saskatchewan. In addition, we share many strong common feelings on the Bill before us and on many other matters. It may be folksy to recollect, but my mother used to toboggan the hill down the coulee into his grandmother's backyard in Saskatchewan, and thus there is a personal connection, though not a direct one, that makes me happy to share this moment with him and to share his feelings and support for this proposition.
On previous occasions when Bills of a similar nature, whether presented by my colleague or by other Members of my Party, the NDP, numerous Members from other Parties have expressed particular misgivings about certain sections, most often because they stated that it would impinge on certain civilian uses of nuclear energy or medical uses of nuclear energy. I want to assure my colleagues that, having read this Bill, all pains have been taken to ensure that those kinds of misgivings may not legitimately be expressed with any degree of legitimacy upon the Bill before us. When Members of the Conservative Party or the Liberal Party rise to speak, for a change they will have to address the substance and the principle rather than finding nitpicking excuses, which I would not suggest is what they would do, but some people in this country from time to time are wont to do.
The Bill before us is short enough, and I intend to read it into the record, if the Speaker will consent. I will not read the penalty provisions because I do not think they are particularly germane to the matter under debate. Let me now read the Bill into the record.
1.	This Act may be cited as the Nuclear Weapons Free Zone Act.
2.	The sovereign nation of Canada, including the territorial coastal waters, inland bodies of water and airspace over which Canada has jurisdiction, is hereby declared to be a nuclear weapons free zone.
3.	(1) No person, corporation, government agency or association of any nature whatsoever shall develop, test, manufacture, import, transport or store any nuclear weapon, nuclear weapons system, nuclear weapons support system, or any components therefor, within Canada, its territorial coastal waters, its inland bodies of water or its airspace over which Canada has jurisdiction for any reason whatsoever, including the defence of Canada or any ally thereof.
The rest of the Bill gets into the penalty provisions and I will not read them at this time.
I think the intent of the Bill is crystal clear. The wording is crystal clear. There is no room for fudging and there is no room for misunderstanding. I hope the debate will have the same degree of clarity as does the Bill.
One of the impacts which such legislation, if it were to become law, would have, would be the cessation not only of the testing of the cruise missile within Canada but also preventing the manufacture of the guidance system or portions of it within Canada as well. In thinking about that subject, I cannot help but digress a little to think of the many times that Members of the Government, including the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Blais) and the former Minister of National Defence have, in
Nuclear Weapons Free Zone Act this House and elsewhere across this land, consistently gone on and on to say that we are testing the cruise missile in Canada because it is a commitment to NATO. They have said that on innumerable occasions and in innumerable ways. That is false. They know that assertion to be false because one or two of them have said on public occasions, I am not sure whether or not in this House, when cross-examined by reporters from the media, that the impression given by those statements was false. I think one can reach no other conclusion other than they have known what they have said. They have since said it repeatedly both in this Chamber and across the land, on television, on radio, at public meetings, and at seminars. It is regrettable that they have never admitted the facts. They know it to be true.
The basic reason we are testing the Cruise missile in Canada, other than for some kind of loyalty oath in a broad sense to the incumbent President of the United States, whatever that happens to be worth, and we all have our own feelings on that, is because this country wants a larger share of defence production in Canada. We are in it for the money. Tommy Douglas used to say-and it is one of the truest things the hon. gentleman ever said-that "Whenever they say it's not the money, it's the principle of the thing, you can always be sure it's the money". That is what cruise testing in Canada is about. Liberal Members know it, Conservative Members know it, and we know it. It is encumbent upon us if we want to disagree to have the intestinal fortitude to tell the public what the debate is about. If we think risking our credibility as a peace-seeking nation with fairly clean credentials is worth a few jobs and a few bucks that will accrue, particularly to Litton Industries, but perhaps to other companies as well, in defence sharing agreements with the United States and perhaps with some of our European allies, then that is a debate we can properly have. Let us debate the issue for what it is. Let us get the issue clear.
I found it galling, to come to more recent events, to watch the Minister of National Defence at a meeting of NATO ministers in Europe just a week ago, particularly considering some of the debate and circumstances which have come to light in this House in the last few days about Canada's willingness or ability to honour its own commitments whether or not we agree with them. He had the unmitigated gall to attend a NATO Ministers' meeting in Europe and blame one of our NATO allies, the Netherlands, for "betraying the NATO Alliance", because it has not yet agreed and it is still undecided,-it has not yet agreed to station U.S. Pershing and U.S. Cruise missiles on its soil. Talk about the pot calling the kettle black!
As I said, we may or may not agree on certain commitments that we have, but I think any Canadian who is a person of honour would say that if we have made a firm commitment, at least we ought to do our best to keep it. It ill behooves anyone who pretends or wants to be called honourable to pursue the kind of shameful course which the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Blais) pursued in Europe just last week.

The House of Representatives of the United States has gone on record favouring a nuclear freeze as a first step. Are they anti-American? The previous votes of politicians which have taken place in this House of Commons on the issues of a nuclear freeze, a disarmament referendum and on the testing of Cruise missiles in Canada are on the record. Sometimes he comes down to earth, but he has some really wierd flights at times too. And, I am not anti-American because I agree with the majority of the Members of the House of Representatives to the South of us.
I agree with many other institutions and organizations throughout the United States which know that in a world like ours we must be able to guarantee a future to our children and our children's children, so that they can decide for themselves what options they will take, whether to live or die, or whether to have a planet left in which to live.
It is beyond the kind of petty politics we have seen here. The Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Minister of National Defence and the former Minister of National Defence have lied to this House and they have lied to this nation continuously. They have deliberately misled this House. They have deliberately misled the Canadian people. They have been called "liars" by my colleagues both inside and outside the House of Commons, but they have not yet had the guts to stand up and admit it.
Let us debate the real issues. Let us debate whether or not risking our credibility and risking our lives is worth the few bucks and the few jobs which Litton Industries will provide. Let us debate that, because that is the issue. Let us make it clear to the Canadian people that the Cruise missile, which is being tested in Canada, with its kind of guidance system, is not for NATO use. are to be used directly-and it is being tested along a track which includes part of its testing field in the constituency of the Hon. Member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake (Mr. Anguish)-so that an air-launched Cruise missile can fly from the Arctic Ocean and follow the tundra track to the industrial heartland of the Soviet Union. That guidance system or that kind of terrain has nothing to do with the method by which Cruise missiles currently being deployed in Europe are to be used or tested. It is a different weapon. We have been receiving false and phoney arguments. The Government does not want the public to know that the Prime Minister has lied, that the Secretary of State for External Affairs has lied, that the Minister of National Defence has lied and that the former Minister of National Defence has lied in this House, and people who lie are liars.

Mr. Speaker, it is of considerable value to us as Members of Parliament and to the public of Canada that this issue be debated in the House of Commons, albeit, at a late hour on Friday afternoon. The whole question of disarmament, particularly nuclear disarmament, is of concern to all Members of Parliament as it is to all Canadians. No one wants war, let alone a nuclear war. I do not think there is one Member of this House who would take a differing view.
A considerable amount of thought has been given to this matter both by elected Members and within the bureaucracy, particularly the Department of External Affairs. When you are part and parcel of the operation of Parliament, you recognize that. Somebody who is not at home here, somebody from the outisde, so to speak, does not understand the amount of thought given to these matters and the amount of expertise that resides amongst the elected and non-elected people within Government in its widest sense. It is not readily apparent.
Nuclear Weapons Free Zone Act
One of our jobs as Members of Parliament is to engage in public debate on these issues so that the people of Canada become aware of the various points of argument and can make up their own minds in these issues and possibly give us some direction. There has, however, been some reluctance, particularly on the Government side, to bring these matters forward. There is a very good reason for this.
First, there are no real specific solutions at this time. The NDP like to think they have specific solutions with instruments such as Private Member's Bill C-203, with which we are dealing this afternoon. However, any careful reflection will show that it is full of holes and rather doomed to failure when looking at a long-term solution to the problem of the arms race.
The Government is unable to put forward to this House specific matters for debate and resolution. It would feel rather foolish bringing something forward of a non-specific nature and, therefore, does not do that. If those who take a rational view of arms control matters take the long view and recognize the amount of hard work that would have to go into any solution, the negotiations that would take place on a continuing basis, they would feel that in the meantime something like to two-track approach as an option would have to be pursued in order to maintain Canada and NATO defence capabilities. These people are sometimes reluctant to engage in discussions on the peace issue because they might be accused of being against peace. Of course, none of us are.
Therefore, it is good on a Friday afternoon to have an opportunity to talk on these matters and try to come up with some potential solution. That is where we are at now. We are in the idea formulation stage rather than bringing forward specific formulae that will enable us, all people in the world, and not just Canada, to come to real solutions.
As I said before, the Bill introduced by the Hon. Member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake (Mr. Anguish) at first blush seems in principle quite reasonable. Certainly he has his heart in the right place. However, when you examine it in detail, you find that it is rather naive and simplistic. It is the facile approach to the issue; kind of a quick-fix solution. In an earlier debate on a related subject, I went at some length into the "Outlawry of War" movement that was prevalent in North America and Europe in the 1920s and in the 1930s. That was another simplistic approach where every nation of the world would sign a treaty not to engage in war. Once they all had signed a solemn pledge, war would be outlawed. There would be no such thing. Of course, we know that that approach failed despite the sincere wishes of many people who thought that would be the solution. We should not make that mistake today. We should work harder to find real and lasting solutions.
What is the present policy of the Government of Canada on the issue of nuclear weapons in Canada? I listened carefully to no less an authority than our Prime Minister (Mr.Trudeau). If I interpret him correctly, it is his wish and early intention that there should not be nuclear weapons on Canadian soil. He does not want to do this because of legislation such as that before
