us, but rather by administrative choice in keeping with the wishes of the people of Canada. We are told that the nuclear weapons presently here will be removed as conventional arms are built up in Canada so that we are able to defend ourselves and keep our NATO commitment by conventional means rather than by nuclear means. This statement is supported by a responsible Opposition in this House.
In keeping with the latter point, we on this side have criticized the Government for some time for the deplorable state of our conventional military equipment. If we do not have sufficient conventional material, we become reliant on nuclear weapons. That is not a good state of affairs. Therefore, I hope that the armed forces of Canada can be properly equipped to counter any hostilities with conventional rather than nuclear weapons.
I do not know whether I should call this an NDP proposal. As far as I know, it reflects not only the individual's private thinking, but also the thinking of the Party he has the honour to represent in this House. If we adopt this proposal, what would be the result? I suspect that a couple of things would happen. First, it would bring about a false sense of security: We do not have nuclear weapons in this country, everybody is working to get rid of them all over the world and therefore we no longer have to worry about the situation. That is an argument that I cannot buy. All you have to do is look not at a map, because maps are usually arranged in an east-west direction laterally, but at a globe to see that Canada is strategically placed mid-way between the two super powers, the U.S.S.R. and the U.S.A. If there is a nuclear warhead-equipped rocket earmarked for the Port of Seattle, you can bet your life there is also one earmarked for the Port of Vancouver. Therefore, if we were to adopt this proposal, the sense of security it might engender would, in my opinion, be entirely false.
Another result of the proposal would be a reliance by Canada almost exclusively for its defence on the United States of America. We need only look back to the Second World War and the illustration of how Great Britain took over Iceland at that time. Iceland was neutral, doing nobody any harm, but it was in a strategic location. Because of the hostilities of the time, the British felt they should set up a military establishment in Iceland. Before that, I do not know whether Iceland had been independent or whether it had been a part of Denmark. However, that is what happened. In all probability, that would occur in Canada if we left ourselves naked and unable to contribute to our defence. In the case of hostilities, I am sure that the Americans would take the same attitude toward Canada as Great Britain took toward Iceland in the last war. I think it is better to retain our options in case hostilities should ever arise, and I think that this could be done within the NATO framework.
You must remember, Mr. Speaker, that NATO is probably one of the first successful peace organizations in the world. That might not become apparent until one really looks into the
matter. NATO was established with the maintenance of peace at heart, and it has been relatively successful. Since its establishment, there has been no major Atlantic conflict. It operates by bringing about peace through deterrence. In the final analysis, deterrence might not be the best way of establishing a lasting peace. However, it is probably better to have peace for several decades in this manner than not to have peace at all. I would encourage Members of the House to be supportive of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
I would suspect that Bill C-203 would be contrary to our treaty obligations regarding both NATO and NORAD. It deals with things like overflights of Canada by our allies and the testing and manufacture of equipment within Canada. We must remember that this Bill deals not only with nuclear weapons themselves, but with any support systems or components therefor. The Bill could conceivably apply to the manufacture in Canada of a half-ton truck if that half-ton truck were ever to be used for the transportation of a nuclear bomb. Perhaps a better example of this would be the aircraft guidance systems. We in Canada are pretty good at making those systems. These of course can be used for both nuclear and non-nuclear weapons systems, and at the same time can have many civil uses.
Another thing I would like to bring to the attention of the House is that in all probability this Bill would prohibit the civil use of nuclear explosives. Although it has not been used to any great extent to the present time, I am sure that nuclear explosives could likely be used in the future for the moving of earth and rock, the construction of canals and for certain mining applications. I understand that the gas-buggy project in the United States was fairly successful in enhancing the permeability of gas-bearing strata and could be used for increased gas supplies.
The dangers associated with radiation from underground use of nuclear explosives is not that great. I understand that with rocks with a fair silica content most of the ensuing radiation is contained in the glass which is created by the fusion of the silica, so there is no great danger of radiation involved. Canadas is one of the countries in the world where, because of large-scale projects which often take place in remote areas, the civil use of nuclear explosives might be of considerable advantage. I would not want to see that possibility jeopardized by the passage of this Bill.
When it comes to establishing nuclear free zones, there is one area of the world in which this might have some advantage at the present time, but only in a limited sense. It might be a practical suggestion for the countries in the Iron Curtain belt in Europe, where the NATO and Warsaw Pact powers are arranged against one another, to be declared a nuclear free zone for tactical nuclear weapons. Of course, strategic weapons with greater range would still be a hazard, but that might be a small step toward the stabilization of that area.
I would like to speak briefly on the second point dealt with in the Bill, which is the idea of a world referendum to be held under the auspices of the United Nations.

Mr. Speaker,
I will only speak for a few minutes. I believe strongly that the motion is supportable and that we should have a nuclear free zone, but I do not think it will happen. I am not sure why we are devoting so much time to this particular problem because, even if we did agreed to it, it would not really change anything in terms of the kind of world in which we live.
I was a member of the NDP years ago. I left basically because I felt that in a political movement of any kind there is a thing called the idea. One gets an idea, one deals with it, and then speaks on it. The other point, which is far more important, is that one must do something to make the idea work. One of the difficulties that I have when I get into a debate on this subject with the NDP is that they have been in opposition for so long, and have been away from the possibility of power for so long, that they really do not understand how to change something or how to do something which is effective.
There is no question in my mind that we are in the most dangerous period in the history of mankind. The International Institute of Strategic Studies in London, England, which is a very conservative organization, made a statement in the last ten days which indicated that we are in nearly as dangerous a situation as we were during the Cuban crisis. There is a very grave danger that a war will occur. If we passed this motion today, it would not change anything. We are up against two superpowers who are not going to move. On our side, that is President Reagan and the administration of the United States. In my opinion, the situation is very, very dangerous in the sense that they are not going to put forward arms control measures that will be workable. The Arms Control Association in the United States,-which includes generals, admirals and people such as Paul Warnke-produced a paper in the last ten days listing five or six reasons why it is certain that the United States Government does not want arms control at this particular time. There is a whole background of information of this kind.
Motions put forward such as the one the NDP has put forward for no first use, no testing of the Cruise and so on are

May 25, 1984
Nuclear Weapons Free Zone Act
admirable, but as soon as they are placed before the Government of the United States the answer is no. As Canadians, how can we be effective in trying to lower the tensions that exist if we keep bringing forward motions which do not have any chance of being effective?
The six powers which have formed the Four Continent Group put forward a motion this week. It is a motion which I support very strongly. However, it was not out on the street for 20 minutes before it was turned down by the Reagan Administration.
It is absolutely essential that we find some way of bringing the Reagan Administration and the Soviet Government-and there is no question that the Soviet group is extremely difficult-together so that they will not make war with each other. The tensions at this stage in the game are beyond any question. We have to worry about the dangers of a war starting from a spark in the Middle East, for examples. I am suggesting one possibility: That we as a Government, with the support of the whole House, adopt a motion that includes the ten points which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has put forward. These ten points are ideas which the Prime Minister gleaned from talking to different countries, including the superpowers and the other three nuclear powers. They involve areas where there is a commonality and where there are common beliefs. We cannot negotiate using techniques which have been used before between the two superpowers. We must start with the common assumptions, which are important assumptions. Assumptions which indicate that we do not want to have insecure or destabilizing weapons. Assumptions, for examples that one side is not going to try and destroy the economy of the other side. These are the things which we must do.
Any motion or statement, however pure and great, will be rejected out of hand by one or the other of the superpowers. They are not going to do anything at this particular point. Therefore, I think the debate today should not be on this particular motion, no matter how well the motion is presented and how desirable it is, but on how we can break the impasse between the two superpowers. I suggest the way that can be done is by starting with the common ground created by the Prime Minister and working toward negotiation which can proceed in a realistic way.

Mr. Speaker, I do not often rise in the House to speak, because there are not many issues
which are pertinent to Arctic people. However, this issue is pertinent because of the testing of the Cruise missile in the Northwest Territories. That is almost directly related to the motion put forward in Bill C-203.
Because of the time limitations, I would like to refer to two resolutions which were passed by the Inuit Circumpolar Conference in 1983 in Frobisher Bay, and previously in 1981 in Greenland. The resolutions deal with nuclear free zones in the Arctic, which is parallel to the motion put forward in Bill C-203.
The first resolution was passed in Greenland by Inuit from around the world. They included members from Alaska, Greenland, Denmark and Canada. Hopefully in the future members from the Soviet Union will participate.
The conference passed a resolution in 1981 which indicated that, whereas radioactive materials are a known hazard to human life and the environment; whereas the Arctic and sub-Arctic regions and particularly fragile ecosystems and environments vital to Inuit subsistence; whereas there are deposits of uranium, thorium, lithium and other materials related to the nuclear industry in the Inuit homeland contemplated for exportation by various southern economic interests; whereas radioactive fall out from nuclear devices more seriously affects the Arctic and sub-Arctic regions than other areas of the world; therefore, be it resolved that the Inuit Circumpolar Conference call upon the Governments of Canada, the United States and Denmark to halt present exploitation for an exportation of uranium, thorium and lithium and other materials related to the nuclear industry in the Inuit homeland; prevent disposal of radioactive waste and materials in the Inuit homeland and prevent testing of nuclear devices in the Inuit homeland.
I would like to refer to the second resolution which was passed in 1983 in Frobisher Bay, but time does not allow me to do so.
